context.heading: A harvest feast fifty days after Passover
context.body: Pentecost (Greek pentēkostē, "fiftieth") is the Feast of Weeks, held fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). It was one of three feasts when Jewish men were expected in Jerusalem, and it thanked God for the firstfruits of the wheat harvest. Luke's timing is pointed: fifty days after Jesus died at Passover, about three thousand people are gathered in as the first harvest of the church. Later Jewish writers also tied the feast to the giving of the law at Sinai, and many readers hear echoes of Sinai's fire and loud sound (Exodus 19:16–19) in this chapter.

context.heading: Wind, breath and Spirit
context.body: The sound is like a mighty rushing wind (pnoē, "breath" or "blast"). In Greek, pneuma means wind, breath and spirit, as Hebrew ruach does, so the sign fits what it announces. Readers who knew the Scriptures would think of God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the wind blowing life into dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9–14) and Jesus' words that the Spirit blows like the wind (John 3:8).

context.heading: Fire that rests on each one
context.body: Fire often marks God's presence in the Old Testament: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, Sinai, and the fire that fell on the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 3:2; 40:38; 2 Chronicles 7:1). John the Baptist promised that the coming one would baptize "with the Holy Spirit and with fire" (Luke 3:16). Here the fire separates and rests on each believer. God's presence is no longer centered on one building but dwells in His people.

context.heading: Real languages the visitors understood
context.body: The crowd hears the disciples in their own dialektos, their native language or dialect (vv. 6, 8). Luke stresses that these were known languages, since visitors from many lands understood them without an interpreter. Many readers see this as a reversal of Babel, where God scattered the nations by confusing their language (Genesis 11:1–9). At Pentecost the nations hear one message, each in its own tongue.

context.heading: Pilgrims from every nation under heaven
context.body: The list runs roughly from Parthia in the east to Rome in the west, with Arabia and Crete at the edges. These were mostly Jews of the dispersion, scattered since the exiles, along with proselytes (Gentiles who had converted to Judaism). The list echoes the table of nations in Genesis 10 and previews the gospel going "to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Some who believed would carry the message home.

context.heading: Joel and the last days
context.body: Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32 and opens it with "in the last days" (eschatos). In the New Testament the last days are the whole age that began with Jesus' resurrection and the Spirit's coming and runs until He returns (Hebrews 1:2). Under the old covenant the Spirit came on chosen prophets, kings and craftsmen. Joel promised the Spirit for sons and daughters, young and old, and even servants, and Peter says that day has come. The cosmic signs in vv. 19–20 use prophetic language for God's coming judgment; Christians read them in different ways, some as fulfilled in part at the cross and Pentecost and some as still to come.

context.heading: David's tomb was still there
context.body: Peter's crowd could walk to David's tomb (mnēma) in Jerusalem; the historian Josephus also mentions it. That is the point of Peter's argument from Psalm 16. David wrote, "You will not let Your Holy One see decay," yet David died and his body decayed. So the psalm must speak of the Messiah, David's descendant, whom God raised. Peter then cites Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often, to show the Messiah would be enthroned at God's right hand.

context.heading: Cut to the heart
context.body: Katanyssō means to pierce or stab sharply. The crowd realizes that the Jesus they rejected weeks earlier is the Lord and Christ (v. 36). Their question, "What shall we do?", shows that the sermon pierced their conscience and did not only inform them. Peter's answer is immediate: repent, be baptized in Jesus' name, and receive the promised Spirit.

context.heading: Devoted to four things
context.body: Proskartereō means to hold fast, persist and keep at something. The same word describes the disciples praying together before Pentecost (Acts 1:14) and meeting daily in the temple (v. 46). The new believers keep at the apostles' teaching, fellowship (koinōnia), the breaking of bread and the prayers. They still went to the temple, since the first Christians were Jews who saw Jesus as the fulfillment of their faith, and they also met in homes.

theology.title: The promise of the Spirit kept
theology.body: Pentecost fulfills what God promised through the prophets (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27) and what Jesus promised His disciples (Luke 24:49; John 14:16–17; Acts 1:4–5). The Spirit had been at work before, but now He is poured out on all God's people to dwell in them and empower their witness. The chapter is also quietly Trinitarian: the Son, exalted to the Father's right hand, receives the promised Spirit from the Father and pours Him out (v. 33).

theology.title: Jesus is Lord and Christ
theology.body: Peter's sermon is about Jesus, not the tongues. God attested Him by miracles (v. 22), God raised Him (vv. 24, 32) and God exalted Him (v. 33), so "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ" (v. 36). In v. 21 Joel's "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord" refers to the LORD, Israel's God. By v. 38 people are baptized in the name of Jesus. The earliest Christian preaching already gives Jesus the name and honor that belong to God.

theology.title: God's plan and human responsibility
theology.body: Jesus was handed over "by God's set plan and foreknowledge," and He was also put to death by lawless hands (v. 23). Scripture holds both together without explaining away either. God's purpose stood behind the cross, and the people who rejected Jesus were truly guilty, which is why they are called to repent. The worst thing humans ever did became the means of their salvation.

theology.title: Repentance, faith and baptism
theology.body: Peter calls for repentance, a turning of the whole life, and baptism in Jesus' name, with the promise of forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit (v. 38). Christians understand how baptism relates to forgiveness in different ways. Many evangelicals see baptism as the public sign of a faith that has already received forgiveness, pointing to passages that tie forgiveness to faith alone (Acts 10:43; 16:31). Other traditions see baptism as a means God uses to give grace. All agree the call is to turn to Christ and be joined to His people, and the promise reaches "all who are far off" (v. 39).

theology.title: Tongues and Spirit baptism: where Christians differ
theology.body: Believers read Pentecost differently. Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians see baptism in the Spirit as an experience distinct from conversion, often marked by speaking in tongues, and expect it today. Many other evangelicals hold that every believer is baptized by the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13). They see Pentecost as a one-time turning point in God's plan, like the cross and resurrection, rather than a pattern each Christian repeats. Christians also differ on whether tongues continue today. Common ground: every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38), and the Spirit's work points to Jesus.

theology.title: A new community
theology.body: The Spirit creates a people as well as changing individuals. The first believers learn from the apostles, share life, eat together, pray, give to anyone in need and worship with glad hearts (vv. 42–47). The sharing was voluntary love, not a required economic system; Acts 5:4 notes that property remained the owner's to keep or give. Luke presents it as a picture of what the Spirit does when He fills a church.

application.title: The Spirit is for ordinary believers
application.body: Joel's promise includes sons and daughters, young and old, and servants. God's Spirit is given to every believer, not only to leaders or especially gifted people. Your faith is meant to be lived in His power, not only your own effort.
application.question: Where have you assumed God works through other people but not through you?

application.title: Let Scripture interpret experience
application.body: Something astonishing happened, and Peter explained it from Joel and the Psalms. He did not build his message on the experience itself. Strong spiritual moments are good gifts, and the Bible tells us what they mean and tests whether they are from God.
application.question: When something stirs you spiritually, how do you weigh it against Scripture?

application.title: Conviction calls for a response
application.body: The crowd was cut to the heart and asked, "What shall we do?" Conviction is God's kindness when it leads us to act. It is not meant to leave us feeling guilty and stuck.
application.question: Is there something God has been pressing on your heart that needs a clear step of obedience this week?

application.title: Keep at the basics
application.body: The first church kept at four simple things: the apostles' teaching (Scripture), fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Spiritual growth comes from steadily practicing these in the company of other believers.
application.question: Which of the four is thinnest in your life right now, and what is one small step to strengthen it?

application.title: Generosity that notices need
application.body: The believers gave to anyone as they had need. The Spirit made them notice one another. Generosity is one of the clearest signs that a church has been changed by the gospel.
application.question: Whose need around you could you help meet this week?
